title: Judges 19:11–21
context: As evening falls, the Levite refuses to stay in Jebus (Jerusalem), a city not yet held by Israel, and presses on to Gibeah in Benjamin, expecting better treatment among fellow Israelites. No one in Gibeah takes the travelers in until an old man from Ephraim, himself an outsider there, offers them his house. The scene sets up a bitter irony: the Israelite town the Levite trusted proves less safe than the foreign city he avoided. Readers in both traditions commonly see the failure of hospitality here as a sign of how far Israel had drifted from God’s law, which called for care for the stranger (Leviticus 19:33; Deuteronomy 10:19). The verses raise no doctrinal division between them.

verses.text: When they were by Jebus, the day was far spent; and the servant said to his master, “Please come and let’s enter into this city of the Jebusites, and stay in it.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the servant’s sensible suggestion to stay in the city of the Jebusites as the day is far spent. Practical wisdom is offered by the one with the least status.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the servant’s counsel as reasonable in light of the danger of travel after dark. Both traditions commonly observe that the Levite’s rejection of this advice carries painful irony.

verses.text: His master said to him, “We won’t enter into the city of a foreigner that is not of the children of Israel; but we will pass over to Gibeah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite refusing to enter a foreign city, expecting safety among fellow Israelites in Gibeah. His assumption will prove tragically wrong.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the irony that the Israelite town will behave worse than the foreign one he avoids. Readers in both traditions commonly see this as part of the narrator’s critique of Israel in this period.

verses.text: He said to his servant, “Come and let’s draw near to one of these places; and we will lodge in Gibeah, or in Ramah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the Levite’s plan to lodge in Gibeah or Ramah. His choices are made with confidence in his own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the verse as narrowing the story toward Gibeah, where the crisis will occur. Both traditions commonly hold the locations of these towns with the caution appropriate to ancient geography.

verses.text: So they passed on and went their way; and the sun went down on them near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the sun going down near Gibeah, which belongs to Benjamin. The detail sets the scene for the evening’s events.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the text identifies Gibeah as Benjamite, preparing for the tribal conflict that follows. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a narrative transition.

verses.text: They went over there, to go in to stay in Gibeah. He went in, and sat down in the street of the city; for there was no one who took them into his house to stay.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that no one in Gibeah takes the travelers in, a serious failure of hospitality. In Israel’s setting, welcoming the stranger was expected and commanded (compare Leviticus 19:33).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the town’s indifference as a symptom of deeper spiritual decline. Both traditions commonly read the verse as an early warning of the moral condition of Gibeah.

verses.text: Behold, an old man came from his work out of the field at evening. Now the man was from the hill country of Ephraim, and he lived in Gibeah; but the men of the place were Benjamites.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the one man who shows kindness is himself from Ephraim, an outsider living in Gibeah. The local men are described simply as Benjamites.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator drawing attention to the contrast between the sojourner and the townsmen. Readers in both traditions commonly note how outsiders sometimes show more righteousness than insiders in Scripture.

verses.text: He lifted up his eyes, and saw the wayfaring man in the street of the city; and the old man said, “Where are you going? Where did you come from?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the old man noticing the wayfarer in the street and asking where he is going. Simple attention to strangers is the first step of hospitality.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see his question as an act of care in a town that has ignored the travelers. Both traditions commonly see this as a brief moment of decency in a dark chapter.

verses.text: He said to him, “We are passing from Bethlehem Judah to the farther side of the hill country of Ephraim. I am from there, and I went to Bethlehem Judah. I am going to the LORD’s house; and there is no one who has taken me into his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the Levite saying he is going to the LORD’s house, yet no one has taken him in. The mention of the LORD’s house underscores the gap between religious identity and actual practice in the story.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Levite’s reference to the LORD’s house as highlighting his role in worship, which makes his later conduct all the more troubling. Readers in both traditions commonly note the narrative’s quiet irony.

verses.text: Yet there is both straw and feed for our donkeys; and there is bread and wine also for me, and for your servant, and for the young man who is with your servants. There is no lack of anything.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite assuring the host that he has provisions for animals and people. He asks only for shelter, not for supplies.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the travelers lack nothing except a safe place to stay. Both traditions commonly read the verse as emphasizing the town’s failure to offer basic shelter.

verses.text: The old man said, “Peace be to you! Just let me supply all your needs, but don’t sleep in the street.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the old man’s greeting of peace and his offer to supply all needs as genuine hospitality. He urges them not to sleep in the street.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see his welcome as reflecting the hospitality God’s law commends (compare Deuteronomy 10:19). Readers in both traditions commonly value this moment, even though the host’s later choices will be gravely wrong.

verses.text: So he brought him into his house, and gave the donkeys fodder. Then they washed their feet, and ate and drank.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the familiar signs of welcome: feeding the donkeys, washing feet, eating and drinking (compare Genesis 18:4). The scene appears safe and peaceful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the calm of this verse as the lull before the violence that follows. Both traditions commonly read the hospitality here as genuine but unable to protect against the evil outside.
